chapter.title: Reading a shop in five numbers

cards.body: Two shops in the bazaar both sell one slice for ₹500. One is a tiny stall cut into 100 slices. The other is a huge store cut into 10 lakh slices. **The price on the tag tells you almost nothing on its own.** A quote page gives you five numbers that turn one price into the size of the shop and what you are paying for its profit.
cards.simpler: Two shops in the bazaar both sell one slice for ₹500. One is a tiny stall cut into 100 slices. The other is a huge store cut into 10 lakh slices. **The price on the tag tells you almost nothing on its own.** Like knowing a cake slice costs ₹500, but not the size of the cake. A quote page gives five numbers that turn one price into the shop's size and what you pay for its profit.

cards.prompt: Two shares. Asha Autos trades at ₹3,000. Bela Biscuits trades at ₹60. Which is the bigger company?

options.text: Asha Autos. A higher price means a bigger company.
Bela Biscuits. Cheap shares mean more people buy, so it must be big.
Cannot tell yet. You need to know how many shares each company has.

whyNot.a: That's the price of one slice, not the size of the shop: a shop cut into few slices has pricey slices.
whyNot.b: That's a guess about popularity, not size: a cheap slice can belong to a huge shop or a tiny one.

cards.reteach: Price is the cost of one slice. Size is the cost of all the slices together. A pizza cut into 4 has big, expensive slices. Cut into 40, small cheap ones. Same pizza.

cards.title: Price and market cap
cards.body:
*Price* is what one share last traded for. It changes every second, as chapter 1 showed, and it only tells you the cost of one slice.

*Market cap* (market capitalisation) is the price multiplied by the total number of shares. **It is the size of the whole shop.** ₹60 a share times 50 crore shares is ₹3,000 crore. ₹3,000 a share times 1 crore shares is also ₹3,000 crore. Same size, very different price tags.

Indian sites sort shops by this: *large cap* for the 100 biggest companies, *mid cap* for the next 150, *small cap* for the rest. Every Nifty 50 company is a large cap.
cards.simpler: *Price* is what one share last sold for. It only tells the cost of one slice. *Market cap* is price times total shares. **It is the size of the whole shop.** ₹60 a share times 50 crore shares is ₹3,000 crore. ₹3,000 a share times 1 crore shares is ₹3,000 crore too. Same size, different tags. Sites sort by size: large cap is the 100 biggest, including every Nifty 50 company, mid cap the next 150, small cap the rest.

cards.title: The wedding tip
cards.body: At a cousin's wedding, Rohan is told a ₹45 share is a bargain and a ₹2,800 share is 'too expensive for people like us'. He opens both quote pages that night. The ₹45 shop has 60 crore shares: market cap ₹2,700 crore, a small cap. The ₹2,800 shop has 250 crore shares: market cap ₹7 lakh crore, one of the biggest in the bazaar. **The 'expensive' slice came from the shop about 260 times larger.**
cards.simpler: At a cousin's wedding, Rohan hears a ₹45 share is a bargain and a ₹2,800 share is 'too expensive for people like us'. That night he opens both quote pages. The ₹45 shop has 60 crore shares, so its market cap is ₹2,700 crore, a small cap. The ₹2,800 shop has 250 crore shares, so its market cap is ₹7 lakh crore, one of the biggest in the bazaar. **The 'expensive' slice came from a shop about 260 times larger.**

cards.prompt: A quote page shows: Price ₹120. Total shares 200 crore. Yearly profit per share ₹10. What is the market cap?

whyNot.a: That's the price with 'crore' stuck on the end, not price times shares: the multiplication got skipped.
whyNot.c: That's price times profit per share, not price times number of shares: profit comes into the P/E on the next card.

cards.reteach: Market cap is the price of one slice times the number of slices. ₹120 times 200 crore slices is ₹24,000 crore. The number of shares is on the same quote page, usually labelled shares outstanding.

cards.title: P/E: years of profit you pay for
cards.body:
Size is one question. The other: **how much are you paying for the shop's profit?**

*EPS* (earnings per share) is the yearly profit divided by the number of shares: the profit behind one slice. *P/E* is the price divided by EPS. A ₹120 share with EPS ₹10 has a P/E of 12. Say it as 'I pay 12 years of today's profit for this slice.' A P/E of 60 means buyers expect profit to grow fast. A P/E of 8 means they expect little, or fear trouble. Compare P/E only with shops in the same trade.

Two smaller numbers round out the page. *52-week high and low*: the top and bottom price of the past year. *Dividend yield*: cash the shop paid out last year, as a percent of today's price.
cards.simpler: **How much do you pay for the shop's profit?** *EPS* is the yearly profit behind one slice. *P/E* is price divided by EPS. A P/E of 12 means paying 12 years of profit for a slice. A P/E of 60 means buyers expect fast growth; 8 means they expect little or fear trouble. Compare P/E only within the same trade. The *52-week high and low* is last year's price range. *Dividend yield* is last year's cash payout as a percent of today's price.

cards.body: Priya sees a share at ₹18, near its 52-week low of ₹17 and far below its high of ₹60, and buys 500 because 'it cannot fall much further'. She never looked at the P/E, which showed only a dash: the shop had made a loss, so there was no profit to divide by. **A price near its 52-week low is a fact about the past year, not a floor.** Spot it in yourself: if you call a share cheap and cannot say its P/E, you have only read the price tag.
cards.simpler: Priya sees a share at ₹18, near its 52-week low of ₹17, far below its high of ₹60. She buys 500 because 'it cannot fall much further'. She never checked the P/E. It showed only a dash: the shop made a loss, with no profit to divide. **A price near its 52-week low is a fact about the past year, not a floor.** If you call a share cheap but cannot say its P/E, you only read the price tag.

cards.prompt: Two hospital chains, same market cap. Dr Mehta's chain has a P/E of 25. Dr Rao's chain has a P/E of 70. Which line is true?

options.text: Dr Rao's chain is the bigger company, because its P/E is higher.
Buyers pay 70 years of today's profit for Dr Rao's slice and 25 for Dr Mehta's. They expect Dr Rao's profit to grow faster.
Dr Mehta's chain is cheaper per share, so it is the better buy.

whyNot.a: That's market cap, not P/E: size comes from price times shares, and the question says both sizes are the same.
whyNot.c: That's the price per share, which you were not given: P/E compares price with profit, and a lower P/E alone does not make a better buy.

cards.reteach: P/E says nothing about size. It says how many years of this year's profit you are paying for one slice. A higher P/E means buyers pay more for each rupee of profit, usually because they expect that profit to grow.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Price is one slice, market cap is the whole shop, and P/E is how many years of profit you pay for a slice.** Glance at the 52-week range for where today sits and the dividend yield for cash paid out, then compare P/E only with shops in the same trade.
cards.simpler: **Price is one slice, market cap is the whole shop, and P/E is how many years of profit you pay for a slice.** Glance at the 52-week range to see where today's price sits in the past year. Glance at the dividend yield to see cash paid out. Then compare P/E only with shops in the same trade.

cards.body: Search 'Reliance share price' on your phone. On the quote card, find market cap and P/E. Say out loud: large or small shop, and how many years of profit the price is.
cards.simpler: Pick up your phone and search 'Reliance share price'. A quote card will appear. **Find two numbers on it: market cap and P/E.** Then say out loud, in your own words: is this a large shop or a small shop, and how many years of today's profit does the price equal?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open any quote page and say whether a company is large or small, and whether its price is high or low against its profit.
